''Kenmu no shinsei'' | conventional_long_name = Kenmu Restoration | common_name = Kenmu Restoration | year_start = 1333 | year_end = 1336 | image_flag = Japanese flag during the Kenmu Restoration.png | flag_border = no | flag = | flag_type = | image_coat =Imperial_Seal_of_Japan.svg | symbol_type = [[:en:Imperial Seal of Japan|Imperial Seal]] | p1 = Kamakura shogunate | flag_p1 = Sasa Rindo.svg | border_p1 = no Imperial Court in Kyoto | p2 = Imperial Court in Kyoto | flag_p2 = Imperial_Seal_of_Japan.svg | border_p2 = no | s1 = Ashikaga shogunate | flag_s1 = Ashikaga_mon.svg | border_s1 = no | s2 = Northern Court | flag_s2 =Imperial_Seal_of_Japan.svg | border_s2 = no | s3 = Southern Court | flag_s3 =Imperial_Seal_of_Japan.svg | border_s3 = no | event_start = [[:en:Genkō War|Genkō War]] begins | date_end = February 23 | event_end= [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] captures [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] | event1 = [[Siege of Kamakura (1333)|Siege of Kamakura]] | date_event1 = May 18, 1333 | capital = [[:en:Heian-kyō|Heian-kyō]] | government_type = [[:en:Absolute monarchy|Absolute monarchy]] | title_leader = [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor]] | leader1 = [[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Go-Daigo]] | year_leader1 = 1318–1339 | representative1 = [[:en:Prince Moriyoshi|Moriyoshi]] | representative2 = [[:en:Prince Narinaga|Narinaga]] | year_representative1 = 1333 | year_representative2 = 1335–1336 | title_representative = ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' | religion = [[Shinbutsu-shūgō]] | common_languages = [[:en:Late Middle Japanese|Late Middle Japanese]] | currency = [[:en:Ryō (Japanese coin)|Ryō]] }} {{History of Japan |periods |image=Emperor-Go-Daigo-by-Ogata-Gekko-1904.png |caption=''[[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]]''
by [[:en:Ogata Gekkō|Ogata Gekkō]], 1890}} The {{nihongo|'''Kenmu Restoration'''|建武の新政|Kenmu no shinsei}} was a three-year period of [[:en:Imperial Court in Kyoto|Imperial]] rule in [[:en:Japanese history|Japanese history]] between the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] from 1333 to 1336.Spelling note: A modified [[:en:Hepburn romanization|Hepburn romanization]] system for Japanese words is used throughout Western publications in a range of languages including [[:en:English language|English]]. Unlike the standard system, it maintains the "''n''" even when it's followed by "[[:en:homorganic consonants|homorganic consonants]]" (e.g., ''shinbun'', not ''shimbun''). The Kenmu Restoration was an effort made by [[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]] to overthrow the ruling [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]] (''de facto'' ruled by [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō clan]]) and restore the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]] to power in Japan, returning to [[:en:civilian government|civilian government]] after 148 years of ''[[:en:De facto|De facto]]'' [[:en:Military government|Military government]] from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]].Sansom 1977: 22-42. Go-Daigo launched the [[:en:Genkō War|Genkō War]] in 1331 against the Kamakura Shogunate but was defeated and forced to [[:en:Exile|Exile]] to the [[:en:Oki Islands|Oki Islands]]. Go-Daigo launched a second uprising, and with the assistance of the [[:en:defector|defected]] Kamakura general [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] and rebel leader [[Nitta Yoshisada]], defeated the Kamakura Shogunate at the [[Siege of Kamakura (1333)|siege of Kamakura]] in 1333. The Imperial House was restored to power but Go-Daigo's policies failed to satisfy his major ''[[:en:Samurai|Samurai]]'' supporters and most Japanese people. The Kenmu Restoration was ultimately overthrown when Takauji became ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' and founded the [[:en:Ashikaga Shogunate|Ashikaga Shogunate]] in 1336, beginning the "[[:en:Nanboku-chō period|Northern and Southern Courts]]" period and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]]. The Kenmu Restoration was the last time the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]] held significant power until the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1868. == Background == The Emperor's role had been usurped by the [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] and [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō]] families ever since [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] had obtained from the Emperor the title of ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' in 1192, ruling thereafter from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]]. For various reasons, the Kamakura shogunate decided to allow two contending imperial lines—known as the [[Southern Court]] or junior line, and the [[:en:Northern Court|Northern Court]] or senior line—to alternate on the throne. The method worked for several successions until a member of the Southern Court ascended to the throne as Emperor Go-Daigo. Go-Daigo wanted to overthrow the shogunate and openly defied Kamakura by naming his own son his heir. In 1331 the shogunate exiled Go-Daigo but loyalist forces, including [[Kusunoki Masashige]], rebelled and came to his support. They were aided by, among others, future ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] who had turned against Kamakura when dispatched to put down Go-Daigo's rebellion. At roughly the same time, [[Nitta Yoshisada]], another eastern chieftain, attacked the shogunate's capital. The shogunate tried to resist his advance: Yoshisada and shogunate forces fought several times along the [[:en:Kamakura Kaidō|Kamakura Kaidō]], for example at {{nihongo|Kotesashigahara|小手差原}}, {{nihongo|Kumegawa|久米河}} (both near today's [[:en:Tokorozawa|Tokorozawa]], [[:en:Saitama Prefecture|Saitama Prefecture]]), and [[:en:Battle of Bubaigawara|Bubaigawara]], in today's [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū]], ever closer to Kamakura. The city was finally reached, [[Siege of Kamakura (1333)|besieged]], and taken. Kamakura would remain for one century the political capital of the [[:en:Kantō region|Kantō region]], but its supremacy as political centre was over. == Objectives of the restoration == When Emperor Go-Daigo ascended the throne in 1318, he immediately manifested his intention to rule without interference from the military in Kamakura. Historical documents show that, disregarding evidence to the contrary, he and his advisers believed that a revival of the Imperial House was possible, and that the Kamakura's shogunate was the greatest and most obvious of the obstacles. Another situation that begged for a solution was the land-ownership problem posed by the manors and their lands (see the article [[shōen]]). The great landowners [[:en:Shugo|Shugo]] (governors) and [[:en:Jitō|Jitō]] (manor's lord), with their political independence and their tax exemptions were impoverishing the government and undermining its authority, and [[Kitabatake Chikafusa]], Go-Daigo's future chief adviser, discussed the situation in his works on succession. Chikafusa admitted that nobody had any intention of abolishing those privileges, so the hope of success on this front was from the beginning clearly very dim. What he planned to replace ''shugo'' and ''jitō'' with is unclear, but he surely had no intention of sharing power with the samurai class. However serious the land ownership problem, Go-Daigo and his advisers made no serious effort to solve it, partly because it was samurai from the manors in the western provinces that had defeated the shogunate for him. In such a situation, any effort to regulate the manors was bound to cause resentment among key allies. == Failure of Go-Daigo's policies == [[File:Emperor Godaigo by Monkan-bō Kōshin.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]]]] The Emperor reclaimed the property of some manors his family had previously lost control of, rewarding them with, among others, Buddhist temples like [[Tō-ji]] and [[:en:Daitoku-ji|Daitoku-ji]] in the hope to obtain their support. He however failed to protect the rights of tenants and workers, whose complaints poured into the monasteries. He did not understand the importance to him of the warrior class either, because he never properly rewarded his minor samurai supporters, as he could have done using lands from the confiscated Hōjō lands, indulging instead in favoritism. These errors are the key to understanding the events of the next few decades. After rewarding religious institutions, he prepared to redistribute Hōjō lands, and samurai came to him in great numbers to lay their claims. The biggest rewards were given to samurai, among them [[Nitta Yoshisada]], the man who had destroyed the Kamakura shogunate, and [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]. In so doing, however, he failed to return control of the provinces to [[Kuge|civilians]]. But he made his greatest error when he failed to properly reward minor warriors who had supported him. The tribunals set up to the purpose were inefficient and too inexperienced for the task, and corruption was rife. Samurai anger was made worse by the fact that Go-Daigo, wanting to build a palace for himself but having no funds, levied extra taxes from the samurai class. A wave of enmity towards the nobility started to run through the country, growing stronger with time. The [[Taiheiki]] also records that, although Takauji and Yoshisada were richly rewarded, the offices of ''shugo'' and ''jito'' in more than fifty [[:en:Provinces of Japan|provinces]] went to nobles and court bureaucrats, leaving no spoils for the warriors.Hall and Duus 1990: 184-7. By the end of 1335 the Emperor and the nobility had lost all support of the warrior class. == Rise of the Ashikaga brothers == [[Image:Ashikaga Takauji Jōdo-ji.jpg|thumb|A portrait of [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] bearing his son [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshiakira|Yoshiakira]]'s cipher]] Go-Daigo wanted to re-establish his rule in Kamakura and the east of the country without sending a ''shōgun'' there, as this was seen as still too dangerous. As a compromise, he sent his six-year-old son Prince Norinaga to [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]] (the eastern part of today's [[Tōhoku region]], stretching from [[:en:Fukushima Prefecture|Fukushima Prefecture]] in the south to [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori Prefecture]] in the north) and nominated him Governor-General of the Mutsu and [[:en:Dewa Province|Dewa Province]]s. In an obvious reply to this move, Ashikaga Takauji's younger brother [[:en:Ashikaga Tadayoshi|Tadayoshi]] without an order from the Emperor escorted another of his sons, eleven-year-old Nariyoshi (a.k.a. Narinaga) to Kamakura, where he installed him as Governor of the [[:en:Kōzuke Province|Kōzuke Province]] with himself as a deputy and de facto ruler.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo 2008: 24–25. The appointment of a warrior to an important post was intended to show the Emperor that the samurai class was not ready for a purely civilian rule. Later, a third son of Go-Daigo's, [[:en:Prince Morinaga|Prince Morinaga]], was appointed ''sei-i taishōgun'' together with his brother Norinaga, a move that immediately aroused [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]'s hostility.Shirai 1976: 301–302.In his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Prince Morinaga was not in fact appointed ''shōgun''. This is surely an error, because contradicted by more recent and reliable sources both in English and Japanese, for example Shirai and Hall. Takauji believed the military class had the right to rule and considered himself not a usurper but, since the Ashikaga descended from a branch of the Minamoto clan, rather a restorer of Minamoto power. When the Hōjō garrison at Rokuhara was destroyed in 1333, he immediately stepped in and installed there his office ([[:en:Bugyō|Bugyō]]sho). It kept order in the city and in general took over the original's function. Extending its authority to controlling travel along highways, issuing passports and exercising rights previously belonging to the shogunate's deputies (the [[:en:Rokuhara Tandai|Rokuhara Tandai]]), Takauji showed he believed that samurai political power must continue. His setting himself apart as a representative of the military made him an aggregation point for the warriors' discontent. Samurai saw him as the man who could bring back the shogunate's heyday, and therefore his strength was superior to that of any other samurai, Nitta Yoshisada included. His only obstacle to the shogunate was Prince Morinaga. == Prince Morinaga == [[Image:Kamakura-gu Treasure.jpg|thumb|Prince Morinaga's statue at [[Kamakura-gū]] in Kamakura]] Prince Morinaga, with his prestige and his devotion to the civilian government cause, was Takauji's natural enemy and could count therefore on the support of his adversaries, among them Nitta Yoshisada, whom Takauji had offended. Tension between the Emperor and the Ashikaga gradually grew, until Takauji had Morinaga arrested on a pretext and first confined him in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], then transported him to Kamakura, where the Prince was kept prisoner until late August 1335. The situation in Kamakura continued to be tense, with Hōjō supporters staging sporadic revolts here and there. In the course of the same year [[Hōjō Tokiyuki]], son of last [[:en:Shikken|regent]] [[:en:Hōjō Takatoki|Takatoki]], tried to re-establish the shogunate by force and defeated Tadayoshi in Musashi, in today's [[:en:Kanagawa Prefecture|Kanagawa Prefecture]]. Tadayoshi had to flee, so before leaving he ordered the beheading of Prince Morinaga. Kamakura was therefore temporarily in Tokiyuki's hands. Heard the news, Takauji asked the Emperor to make him ''sei-i tai-shōgun'' so that he could quell the revolt and help his brother. When his request was denied, Takauji organized his forces and returned to Kamakura without the Emperor's permission, defeating the Hōjō.{{efn|Unlike every other source consulted Goble,{{sfn|Goble|1996}} on page 38 of his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Tokiyuki was killed on September 8, 1335 by Ashikaga forces entering Kamakura. This is also certainly an error.}} He then installed himself in Kamakura's [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]] neighborhood.Sansom says Ashikaga was staying at a temple called Eifuku-ji. This is an error, because Takauji in 1335 is known to have stayed at the ''[[:en:Bettō|Bettō]]'s'' residence at {{nihongo|[[Nikaidō#Etimology of the name|Yōfuku-ji]]|永福寺}}, a famous temple in Nikaidō built by Minamoto no Yoritomo which disappeared at some point during the 15th century. Yōfuku-ji was a traditional vacation residence of the ''shōguns'', and the characters in its name are indeed usually read "Eifuku-ji". See the article [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]]. When invited to return to Kyoto, he let it be known through his brother Tadayoshi that he felt safer where he was, and started to build himself a mansion in [[:en:Ōkura Bakufu|Ōkura]], where first Kamakura ''shōgun'' [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s residence had been. == Civil war == Kyoto by then was aware that Takauji had assumed wide powers without imperial permission, for example nominating an [[Uesugi clan]] member to the post of Constable of Kōzuke, Nitta Yoshisada's native province. By late 1335 several thousand of the emperor's men were ready to go to Kamakura, while a great army at the command of [[:en:Kō no Moroyasu|Kō no Moroyasu]] was rushing there to help it resist the attack. On November 17, 1335, Tadayoshi issued a message in his brother's name asking all samurai to join the Ashikaga and destroy Nitta Yoshisada. The Court, meanwhile, had done the opposite, ordering samurai from all provinces to join Yoshisada and destroy the two Ashikaga. The war started with most samurai convinced that Takauji was the man they needed to have their grievances redressed, and most peasants were persuaded that they had been better off under the shogunate. The campaign was therefore enormously successful for the Ashikaga, with huge numbers of samurai rushing to join the two brothers. By February 23 of the following year Nitta Yoshisada and the Emperor had lost, and Kyoto itself had fallen. On February 25, 1336, Ashikaga Takauji entered the capital and the Kenmu Restoration ended. == Calendrical peculiarities of the era == The [[:en:Kenmu|Kenmu]] era is in the anomalous condition of having two different durations. Because [[:en:Japanese era name|Japanese era name]]s (''nengō'') change with the Emperor and the Imperial House split in two after 1336, the Kenmu era was counted by the two sides in two different ways. ''"Kenmu"'' is the era after the [[:en:Genkō (second)|Genkō]] era, and it is understood to have spanned the years 1334 through 1336 before the beginning of the ''"[[:en:Engen|Engen]]"'' era, as time was reckoned by the Southern Court; and it is concurrently said to have spanned the years 1334 through 1338 before [[:en:Ryakuō|Ryakuō]], as time was reckoned by the rival Northern Court. Because the Southern Court, the loser, is nonetheless considered the legitimate one, its time reckoning is the one used by historians. == See also == * [[List of the Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration|Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration]] == Notes == {{notelist|1}} {{reflist|2}} == References == * {{cite book |last1=Hall| first1=John Whitney |last2=Duus |first2=Peter |title=The Cambridge History of Japan |editor=Yamamura Kozo |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-521-22354-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nT9CI5YQF_4C&q=kubo+kanto&pg=PA232}} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | year = 2008 | location = Kamakura, Japan | language = ja | isbn = 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} * {{cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan (3-volume boxed set) |publisher=Charles E. by [[:en:Ogata Gekkō|Ogata Gekkō]], 1890}} The {{nihongo|'''Kenmu Restoration'''|建武の新政|Kenmu no shinsei}} was a three-year period of [[:en:Imperial Court in Kyoto|Imperial]] rule in [[:en:Japanese history|Japanese history]] between the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] from 1333 to 1336.Spelling note: A modified [[:en:Hepburn romanization|Hepburn romanization]] system for Japanese words is used throughout Western publications in a range of languages including [[:en:English language|English]]. Unlike the standard system, it maintains the "''n''" even when it's followed by "[[:en:homorganic consonants|homorganic consonants]]" (e.g., ''shinbun'', not ''shimbun''). The Kenmu Restoration was an effort made by [[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]] to overthrow the ruling [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]] (''de facto'' ruled by [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō clan]]) and restore the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]] to power in Japan, returning to [[:en:civilian government|civilian government]] after 148 years of ''[[:en:De facto|De facto]]'' [[:en:Military government|Military government]] from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]].Sansom 1977: 22-42. Go-Daigo launched the [[:en:Genkō War|Genkō War]] in 1331 against the Kamakura Shogunate but was defeated and forced to [[:en:Exile|Exile]] to the [[:en:Oki Islands|Oki Islands]]. Go-Daigo launched a second uprising, and with the assistance of the [[:en:defector|defected]] Kamakura general [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] and rebel leader [[Nitta Yoshisada]], defeated the Kamakura Shogunate at the [[:en:Siege of Kamakura (1333)|siege of Kamakura]] in 1333. The Imperial House was restored to power but Go-Daigo's policies failed to satisfy his major ''[[:en:Samurai|Samurai]]'' supporters and most Japanese people. The Kenmu Restoration was ultimately overthrown when Takauji became ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' and founded the [[:en:Ashikaga Shogunate|Ashikaga Shogunate]] in 1336, beginning the "[[:en:Nanboku-chō period|Northern and Southern Courts]]" period and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]]. The Kenmu Restoration was the last time the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]] held significant power until the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1868. == Background == The Emperor's role had been usurped by the [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] and [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō]] families ever since [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] had obtained from the Emperor the title of ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' in 1192, ruling thereafter from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]]. For various reasons, the Kamakura shogunate decided to allow two contending imperial lines—known as the [[Southern Court]] or junior line, and the [[:en:Northern Court|Northern Court]] or senior line—to alternate on the throne. The method worked for several successions until a member of the Southern Court ascended to the throne as Emperor Go-Daigo. Go-Daigo wanted to overthrow the shogunate and openly defied Kamakura by naming his own son his heir. In 1331 the shogunate exiled Go-Daigo but loyalist forces, including [[Kusunoki Masashige]], rebelled and came to his support. They were aided by, among others, future ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] who had turned against Kamakura when dispatched to put down Go-Daigo's rebellion. At roughly the same time, [[Nitta Yoshisada]], another eastern chieftain, attacked the shogunate's capital. The shogunate tried to resist his advance: Yoshisada and shogunate forces fought several times along the [[:en:Kamakura Kaidō|Kamakura Kaidō]], for example at {{nihongo|Kotesashigahara|小手差原}}, {{nihongo|Kumegawa|久米河}} (both near today's [[:en:Tokorozawa|Tokorozawa]], [[:en:Saitama Prefecture|Saitama Prefecture]]), and [[:en:Battle of Bubaigawara|Bubaigawara]], in today's [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū]], ever closer to Kamakura. The city was finally reached, [[:en:Siege of Kamakura (1333)|besieged]], and taken. Kamakura would remain for one century the political capital of the [[:en:Kantō region|Kantō region]], but its supremacy as political centre was over. == Objectives of the restoration == When Emperor Go-Daigo ascended the throne in 1318, he immediately manifested his intention to rule without interference from the military in Kamakura. Historical documents show that, disregarding evidence to the contrary, he and his advisers believed that a revival of the Imperial House was possible, and that the Kamakura's shogunate was the greatest and most obvious of the obstacles. Another situation that begged for a solution was the land-ownership problem posed by the manors and their lands (see the article [[shōen]]). The great landowners [[:en:Shugo|Shugo]] (governors) and [[:en:Jitō|Jitō]] (manor's lord), with their political independence and their tax exemptions were impoverishing the government and undermining its authority, and [[Kitabatake Chikafusa]], Go-Daigo's future chief adviser, discussed the situation in his works on succession. Chikafusa admitted that nobody had any intention of abolishing those privileges, so the hope of success on this front was from the beginning clearly very dim. What he planned to replace ''shugo'' and ''jitō'' with is unclear, but he surely had no intention of sharing power with the samurai class. However serious the land ownership problem, Go-Daigo and his advisers made no serious effort to solve it, partly because it was samurai from the manors in the western provinces that had defeated the shogunate for him. In such a situation, any effort to regulate the manors was bound to cause resentment among key allies. == Failure of Go-Daigo's policies == [[File:Emperor Godaigo by Monkan-bō Kōshin.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]]]] The Emperor reclaimed the property of some manors his family had previously lost control of, rewarding them with, among others, Buddhist temples like [[Tō-ji]] and [[:en:Daitoku-ji|Daitoku-ji]] in the hope to obtain their support. He however failed to protect the rights of tenants and workers, whose complaints poured into the monasteries. He did not understand the importance to him of the warrior class either, because he never properly rewarded his minor samurai supporters, as he could have done using lands from the confiscated Hōjō lands, indulging instead in favoritism. These errors are the key to understanding the events of the next few decades. After rewarding religious institutions, he prepared to redistribute Hōjō lands, and samurai came to him in great numbers to lay their claims. The biggest rewards were given to samurai, among them [[Nitta Yoshisada]], the man who had destroyed the Kamakura shogunate, and [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]. In so doing, however, he failed to return control of the provinces to [[Kuge|civilians]]. But he made his greatest error when he failed to properly reward minor warriors who had supported him. The tribunals set up to the purpose were inefficient and too inexperienced for the task, and corruption was rife. Samurai anger was made worse by the fact that Go-Daigo, wanting to build a palace for himself but having no funds, levied extra taxes from the samurai class. A wave of enmity towards the nobility started to run through the country, growing stronger with time. The [[Taiheiki]] also records that, although Takauji and Yoshisada were richly rewarded, the offices of ''shugo'' and ''jito'' in more than fifty [[:en:Provinces of Japan|provinces]] went to nobles and court bureaucrats, leaving no spoils for the warriors.Hall and Duus 1990: 184-7. By the end of 1335 the Emperor and the nobility had lost all support of the warrior class. == Rise of the Ashikaga brothers == [[Image:Ashikaga Takauji Jōdo-ji.jpg|thumb|A portrait of [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] bearing his son [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshiakira|Yoshiakira]]'s cipher]] Go-Daigo wanted to re-establish his rule in Kamakura and the east of the country without sending a ''shōgun'' there, as this was seen as still too dangerous. As a compromise, he sent his six-year-old son Prince Norinaga to [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]] (the eastern part of today's [[Tōhoku region]], stretching from [[:en:Fukushima Prefecture|Fukushima Prefecture]] in the south to [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori Prefecture]] in the north) and nominated him Governor-General of the Mutsu and [[:en:Dewa Province|Dewa Province]]s. In an obvious reply to this move, Ashikaga Takauji's younger brother [[:en:Ashikaga Tadayoshi|Tadayoshi]] without an order from the Emperor escorted another of his sons, eleven-year-old Nariyoshi (a.k.a. Narinaga) to Kamakura, where he installed him as Governor of the [[:en:Kōzuke Province|Kōzuke Province]] with himself as a deputy and de facto ruler.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo 2008: 24–25. The appointment of a warrior to an important post was intended to show the Emperor that the samurai class was not ready for a purely civilian rule. Later, a third son of Go-Daigo's, [[:en:Prince Morinaga|Prince Morinaga]], was appointed ''sei-i taishōgun'' together with his brother Norinaga, a move that immediately aroused [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]'s hostility.Shirai 1976: 301–302.In his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Prince Morinaga was not in fact appointed ''shōgun''. This is surely an error, because contradicted by more recent and reliable sources both in English and Japanese, for example Shirai and Hall. Takauji believed the military class had the right to rule and considered himself not a usurper but, since the Ashikaga descended from a branch of the Minamoto clan, rather a restorer of Minamoto power. When the Hōjō garrison at Rokuhara was destroyed in 1333, he immediately stepped in and installed there his office ([[:en:Bugyō|Bugyō]]sho). It kept order in the city and in general took over the original's function. Extending its authority to controlling travel along highways, issuing passports and exercising rights previously belonging to the shogunate's deputies (the [[:en:Rokuhara Tandai|Rokuhara Tandai]]), Takauji showed he believed that samurai political power must continue. His setting himself apart as a representative of the military made him an aggregation point for the warriors' discontent. Samurai saw him as the man who could bring back the shogunate's heyday, and therefore his strength was superior to that of any other samurai, Nitta Yoshisada included. His only obstacle to the shogunate was Prince Morinaga. == Prince Morinaga == [[Image:Kamakura-gu Treasure.jpg|thumb|Prince Morinaga's statue at [[Kamakura-gū]] in Kamakura]] Prince Morinaga, with his prestige and his devotion to the civilian government cause, was Takauji's natural enemy and could count therefore on the support of his adversaries, among them Nitta Yoshisada, whom Takauji had offended. Tension between the Emperor and the Ashikaga gradually grew, until Takauji had Morinaga arrested on a pretext and first confined him in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], then transported him to Kamakura, where the Prince was kept prisoner until late August 1335. The situation in Kamakura continued to be tense, with Hōjō supporters staging sporadic revolts here and there. In the course of the same year [[Hōjō Tokiyuki]], son of last [[:en:Shikken|regent]] [[:en:Hōjō Takatoki|Takatoki]], tried to re-establish the shogunate by force and defeated Tadayoshi in Musashi, in today's [[:en:Kanagawa Prefecture|Kanagawa Prefecture]]. Tadayoshi had to flee, so before leaving he ordered the beheading of Prince Morinaga. Kamakura was therefore temporarily in Tokiyuki's hands. Heard the news, Takauji asked the Emperor to make him ''sei-i tai-shōgun'' so that he could quell the revolt and help his brother. When his request was denied, Takauji organized his forces and returned to Kamakura without the Emperor's permission, defeating the Hōjō.{{efn|Unlike every other source consulted Goble,{{sfn|Goble|1996}} on page 38 of his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Tokiyuki was killed on September 8, 1335 by Ashikaga forces entering Kamakura. This is also certainly an error.}} He then installed himself in Kamakura's [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]] neighborhood.Sansom says Ashikaga was staying at a temple called Eifuku-ji. This is an error, because Takauji in 1335 is known to have stayed at the ''[[:en:Bettō|Bettō]]'s'' residence at {{nihongo|[[Nikaidō#Etimology of the name|Yōfuku-ji]]|永福寺}}, a famous temple in Nikaidō built by Minamoto no Yoritomo which disappeared at some point during the 15th century. Yōfuku-ji was a traditional vacation residence of the ''shōguns'', and the characters in its name are indeed usually read "Eifuku-ji". See the article [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]]. When invited to return to Kyoto, he let it be known through his brother Tadayoshi that he felt safer where he was, and started to build himself a mansion in [[:en:Ōkura Bakufu|Ōkura]], where first Kamakura ''shōgun'' [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s residence had been. == Civil war == Kyoto by then was aware that Takauji had assumed wide powers without imperial permission, for example nominating an [[Uesugi clan]] member to the post of Constable of Kōzuke, Nitta Yoshisada's native province. By late 1335 several thousand of the emperor's men were ready to go to Kamakura, while a great army at the command of [[:en:Kō no Moroyasu|Kō no Moroyasu]] was rushing there to help it resist the attack. On November 17, 1335, Tadayoshi issued a message in his brother's name asking all samurai to join the Ashikaga and destroy Nitta Yoshisada. The Court, meanwhile, had done the opposite, ordering samurai from all provinces to join Yoshisada and destroy the two Ashikaga. The war started with most samurai convinced that Takauji was the man they needed to have their grievances redressed, and most peasants were persuaded that they had been better off under the shogunate. The campaign was therefore enormously successful for the Ashikaga, with huge numbers of samurai rushing to join the two brothers. By February 23 of the following year Nitta Yoshisada and the Emperor had lost, and Kyoto itself had fallen. On February 25, 1336, Ashikaga Takauji entered the capital and the Kenmu Restoration ended. == Calendrical peculiarities of the era == The [[:en:Kenmu|Kenmu]] era is in the anomalous condition of having two different durations. Because [[:en:Japanese era name|Japanese era name]]s (''nengō'') change with the Emperor and the Imperial House split in two after 1336, the Kenmu era was counted by the two sides in two different ways. ''"Kenmu"'' is the era after the [[:en:Genkō (second)|Genkō]] era, and it is understood to have spanned the years 1334 through 1336 before the beginning of the ''"[[:en:Engen|Engen]]"'' era, as time was reckoned by the Southern Court; and it is concurrently said to have spanned the years 1334 through 1338 before [[:en:Ryakuō|Ryakuō]], as time was reckoned by the rival Northern Court. Because the Southern Court, the loser, is nonetheless considered the legitimate one, its time reckoning is the one used by historians. == See also == * [[List of the Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration|Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration]] == Notes == {{notelist|1}} {{reflist|2}} == References == * {{cite book |last1=Hall| first1=John Whitney |last2=Duus |first2=Peter |title=The Cambridge History of Japan |editor=Yamamura Kozo |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-521-22354-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nT9CI5YQF_4C&q=kubo+kanto&pg=PA232}} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | year = 2008 | location = Kamakura, Japan | language = ja | isbn = 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} * {{cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan (3-volume boxed set) |publisher=Charles E. The shogunate tried to resist his advance: Yoshisada and shogunate forces fought several times along the [[:en:Kamakura Kaidō|Kamakura Kaidō]], for example at {{nihongo|Kotesashigahara|小手差原}}, {{nihongo|Kumegawa|久米河}} (both near today's [[:en:Tokorozawa|Tokorozawa]], [[:en:Saitama Prefecture|Saitama Prefecture]]), and [[:en:Battle of Bubaigawara|Bubaigawara]], in today's [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū]], ever closer to Kamakura. The city was finally reached, [[:en:Siege of Kamakura (1333)|besieged]], and taken. Kamakura would remain for one century the political capital of the [[:en:Kantō region|Kantō region]], but its supremacy as political centre was over. == Objectives of the restoration == When Emperor Go-Daigo ascended the throne in 1318, he immediately manifested his intention to rule without interference from the military in Kamakura. Historical documents show that, disregarding evidence to the contrary, he and his advisers believed that a revival of the Imperial House was possible, and that the Kamakura's shogunate was the greatest and most obvious of the obstacles. Another situation that begged for a solution was the land-ownership problem posed by the manors and their lands (see the article [[shōen]]). The great landowners [[:en:Shugo|Shugo]] (governors) and [[:en:Jitō|Jitō]] (manor's lord), with their political independence and their tax exemptions were impoverishing the government and undermining its authority, and [[Kitabatake Chikafusa]], Go-Daigo's future chief adviser, discussed the situation in his works on succession. Chikafusa admitted that nobody had any intention of abolishing those privileges, so the hope of success on this front was from the beginning clearly very dim. What he planned to replace ''shugo'' and ''jitō'' with is unclear, but he surely had no intention of sharing power with the samurai class. However serious the land ownership problem, Go-Daigo and his advisers made no serious effort to solve it, partly because it was samurai from the manors in the western provinces that had defeated the shogunate for him. In such a situation, any effort to regulate the manors was bound to cause resentment among key allies. == Failure of Go-Daigo's policies == [[File:Emperor Godaigo by Monkan-bō Kōshin.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]]]] The Emperor reclaimed the property of some manors his family had previously lost control of, rewarding them with, among others, Buddhist temples like [[Tō-ji]] and [[:en:Daitoku-ji|Daitoku-ji]] in the hope to obtain their support. He however failed to protect the rights of tenants and workers, whose complaints poured into the monasteries. He did not understand the importance to him of the warrior class either, because he never properly rewarded his minor samurai supporters, as he could have done using lands from the confiscated Hōjō lands, indulging instead in favoritism. These errors are the key to understanding the events of the next few decades. After rewarding religious institutions, he prepared to redistribute Hōjō lands, and samurai came to him in great numbers to lay their claims. The biggest rewards were given to samurai, among them [[Nitta Yoshisada]], the man who had destroyed the Kamakura shogunate, and [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]. In so doing, however, he failed to return control of the provinces to [[Kuge|civilians]]. But he made his greatest error when he failed to properly reward minor warriors who had supported him. The tribunals set up to the purpose were inefficient and too inexperienced for the task, and corruption was rife. Samurai anger was made worse by the fact that Go-Daigo, wanting to build a palace for himself but having no funds, levied extra taxes from the samurai class. A wave of enmity towards the nobility started to run through the country, growing stronger with time. The [[Taiheiki]] also records that, although Takauji and Yoshisada were richly rewarded, the offices of ''shugo'' and ''jito'' in more than fifty [[:en:Provinces of Japan|provinces]] went to nobles and court bureaucrats, leaving no spoils for the warriors.Hall and Duus 1990: 184-7. By the end of 1335 the Emperor and the nobility had lost all support of the warrior class. == Rise of the Ashikaga brothers == [[Image:Ashikaga Takauji Jōdo-ji.jpg|thumb|A portrait of [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] bearing his son [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshiakira|Yoshiakira]]'s cipher]] Go-Daigo wanted to re-establish his rule in Kamakura and the east of the country without sending a ''shōgun'' there, as this was seen as still too dangerous. As a compromise, he sent his six-year-old son Prince Norinaga to [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]] (the eastern part of today's [[:en:Tōhoku region|Tōhoku region]], stretching from [[:en:Fukushima Prefecture|Fukushima Prefecture]] in the south to [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori Prefecture]] in the north) and nominated him Governor-General of the Mutsu and [[:en:Dewa Province|Dewa Province]]s. In an obvious reply to this move, Ashikaga Takauji's younger brother [[:en:Ashikaga Tadayoshi|Tadayoshi]] without an order from the Emperor escorted another of his sons, eleven-year-old Nariyoshi (a.k.a. Narinaga) to Kamakura, where he installed him as Governor of the [[:en:Kōzuke Province|Kōzuke Province]] with himself as a deputy and de facto ruler.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo 2008: 24–25. The appointment of a warrior to an important post was intended to show the Emperor that the samurai class was not ready for a purely civilian rule. Later, a third son of Go-Daigo's, [[:en:Prince Morinaga|Prince Morinaga]], was appointed ''sei-i taishōgun'' together with his brother Norinaga, a move that immediately aroused [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]'s hostility.Shirai 1976: 301–302.In his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Prince Morinaga was not in fact appointed ''shōgun''. This is surely an error, because contradicted by more recent and reliable sources both in English and Japanese, for example Shirai and Hall. Takauji believed the military class had the right to rule and considered himself not a usurper but, since the Ashikaga descended from a branch of the Minamoto clan, rather a restorer of Minamoto power. When the Hōjō garrison at Rokuhara was destroyed in 1333, he immediately stepped in and installed there his office ([[:en:Bugyō|Bugyō]]sho). It kept order in the city and in general took over the original's function. Extending its authority to controlling travel along highways, issuing passports and exercising rights previously belonging to the shogunate's deputies (the [[:en:Rokuhara Tandai|Rokuhara Tandai]]), Takauji showed he believed that samurai political power must continue. His setting himself apart as a representative of the military made him an aggregation point for the warriors' discontent. Samurai saw him as the man who could bring back the shogunate's heyday, and therefore his strength was superior to that of any other samurai, Nitta Yoshisada included. His only obstacle to the shogunate was Prince Morinaga. == Prince Morinaga == [[Image:Kamakura-gu Treasure.jpg|thumb|Prince Morinaga's statue at [[Kamakura-gū]] in Kamakura]] Prince Morinaga, with his prestige and his devotion to the civilian government cause, was Takauji's natural enemy and could count therefore on the support of his adversaries, among them Nitta Yoshisada, whom Takauji had offended. Tension between the Emperor and the Ashikaga gradually grew, until Takauji had Morinaga arrested on a pretext and first confined him in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], then transported him to Kamakura, where the Prince was kept prisoner until late August 1335. The situation in Kamakura continued to be tense, with Hōjō supporters staging sporadic revolts here and there. In the course of the same year [[Hōjō Tokiyuki]], son of last [[:en:Shikken|regent]] [[:en:Hōjō Takatoki|Takatoki]], tried to re-establish the shogunate by force and defeated Tadayoshi in Musashi, in today's [[:en:Kanagawa Prefecture|Kanagawa Prefecture]]. Tadayoshi had to flee, so before leaving he ordered the beheading of Prince Morinaga. Kamakura was therefore temporarily in Tokiyuki's hands. Heard the news, Takauji asked the Emperor to make him ''sei-i tai-shōgun'' so that he could quell the revolt and help his brother. When his request was denied, Takauji organized his forces and returned to Kamakura without the Emperor's permission, defeating the Hōjō.{{efn|Unlike every other source consulted Goble,{{sfn|Goble|1996}} on page 38 of his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Tokiyuki was killed on September 8, 1335 by Ashikaga forces entering Kamakura. This is also certainly an error.}} He then installed himself in Kamakura's [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]] neighborhood.Sansom says Ashikaga was staying at a temple called Eifuku-ji. This is an error, because Takauji in 1335 is known to have stayed at the ''[[:en:Bettō|Bettō]]'s'' residence at {{nihongo|[[Nikaidō#Etimology of the name|Yōfuku-ji]]|永福寺}}, a famous temple in Nikaidō built by Minamoto no Yoritomo which disappeared at some point during the 15th century. Yōfuku-ji was a traditional vacation residence of the ''shōguns'', and the characters in its name are indeed usually read "Eifuku-ji". See the article [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]]. When invited to return to Kyoto, he let it be known through his brother Tadayoshi that he felt safer where he was, and started to build himself a mansion in [[:en:Ōkura Bakufu|Ōkura]], where first Kamakura ''shōgun'' [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s residence had been. == Civil war == Kyoto by then was aware that Takauji had assumed wide powers without imperial permission, for example nominating an [[Uesugi clan]] member to the post of Constable of Kōzuke, Nitta Yoshisada's native province. By late 1335 several thousand of the emperor's men were ready to go to Kamakura, while a great army at the command of [[:en:Kō no Moroyasu|Kō no Moroyasu]] was rushing there to help it resist the attack. On November 17, 1335, Tadayoshi issued a message in his brother's name asking all samurai to join the Ashikaga and destroy Nitta Yoshisada. The Court, meanwhile, had done the opposite, ordering samurai from all provinces to join Yoshisada and destroy the two Ashikaga. The war started with most samurai convinced that Takauji was the man they needed to have their grievances redressed, and most peasants were persuaded that they had been better off under the shogunate. The campaign was therefore enormously successful for the Ashikaga, with huge numbers of samurai rushing to join the two brothers. By February 23 of the following year Nitta Yoshisada and the Emperor had lost, and Kyoto itself had fallen. On February 25, 1336, Ashikaga Takauji entered the capital and the Kenmu Restoration ended. == Calendrical peculiarities of the era == The [[:en:Kenmu|Kenmu]] era is in the anomalous condition of having two different durations. Because [[:en:Japanese era name|Japanese era name]]s (''nengō'') change with the Emperor and the Imperial House split in two after 1336, the Kenmu era was counted by the two sides in two different ways. ''"Kenmu"'' is the era after the [[:en:Genkō (second)|Genkō]] era, and it is understood to have spanned the years 1334 through 1336 before the beginning of the ''"[[:en:Engen|Engen]]"'' era, as time was reckoned by the Southern Court; and it is concurrently said to have spanned the years 1334 through 1338 before [[:en:Ryakuō|Ryakuō]], as time was reckoned by the rival Northern Court. Because the Southern Court, the loser, is nonetheless considered the legitimate one, its time reckoning is the one used by historians. == See also == * [[List of the Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration|Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration]] == Notes == {{notelist|1}} {{reflist|2}} == References == * {{cite book |last1=Hall| first1=John Whitney |last2=Duus |first2=Peter |title=The Cambridge History of Japan |editor=Yamamura Kozo |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-521-22354-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nT9CI5YQF_4C&q=kubo+kanto&pg=PA232}} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | year = 2008 | location = Kamakura, Japan | language = ja | isbn = 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} * {{cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan (3-volume boxed set) |publisher=Charles E. by [[:en:Ogata Gekkō|Ogata Gekkō]], 1890}} The {{nihongo|'''Kenmu Restoration'''|建武の新政|Kenmu no shinsei}} was a three-year period of [[:en:Imperial Court in Kyoto|Imperial]] rule in [[:en:Japanese history|Japanese history]] between the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] from 1333 to 1336.Spelling note: A modified [[:en:Hepburn romanization|Hepburn romanization]] system for Japanese words is used throughout Western publications in a range of languages including [[:en:English language|English]]. Unlike the standard system, it maintains the "''n''" even when it's followed by "[[:en:homorganic consonants|homorganic consonants]]" (e.g., ''shinbun'', not ''shimbun''). The Kenmu Restoration was an effort made by [[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]] to overthrow the ruling [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]] (''de facto'' ruled by [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō clan]]) and restore the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]] to power in Japan, returning to [[:en:civilian government|civilian government]] after 148 years of ''[[:en:De facto|De facto]]'' [[:en:Military government|Military government]] from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]].Sansom 1977: 22-42. Go-Daigo launched the [[:en:Genkō War|Genkō War]] in 1331 against the Kamakura Shogunate but was defeated and forced to [[:en:Exile|Exile]] to the [[:en:Oki Islands|Oki Islands]]. Go-Daigo launched a second uprising, and with the assistance of the [[:en:defector|defected]] Kamakura general [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] and rebel leader [[Nitta Yoshisada]], defeated the Kamakura Shogunate at the [[:en:Siege of Kamakura (1333)|siege of Kamakura]] in 1333. The Imperial House was restored to power but Go-Daigo's policies failed to satisfy his major ''[[:en:Samurai|Samurai]]'' supporters and most Japanese people. The Kenmu Restoration was ultimately overthrown when Takauji became ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' and founded the [[:en:Ashikaga Shogunate|Ashikaga Shogunate]] in 1336, beginning the "[[:en:Nanboku-chō period|Northern and Southern Courts]]" period and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]]. The method worked for several successions until a member of the Southern Court ascended to the throne as Emperor Go-Daigo. Go-Daigo wanted to overthrow the shogunate and openly defied Kamakura by naming his own son his heir. In 1331 the shogunate exiled Go-Daigo but loyalist forces, including [[Kusunoki Masashige]], rebelled and came to his support. They were aided by, among others, future ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] who had turned against Kamakura when dispatched to put down Go-Daigo's rebellion. This is surely an error, because contradicted by more recent and reliable sources both in English and Japanese, for example Shirai and Hall. Takauji believed the military class had the right to rule and considered himself not a usurper but, since the Ashikaga descended from a branch of the Minamoto clan, rather a restorer of Minamoto power. When the Hōjō garrison at Rokuhara was destroyed in 1333, he immediately stepped in and installed there his office ([[:en:Bugyō|Bugyō]]sho). It kept order in the city and in general took over the original's function. Extending its authority to controlling travel along highways, issuing passports and exercising rights previously belonging to the shogunate's deputies (the [[:en:Rokuhara Tandai|Rokuhara Tandai]]), Takauji showed he believed that samurai political power must continue. His setting himself apart as a representative of the military made him an aggregation point for the warriors' discontent. Samurai saw him as the man who could bring back the shogunate's heyday, and therefore his strength was superior to that of any other samurai, Nitta Yoshisada included. His only obstacle to the shogunate was Prince Morinaga. == Prince Morinaga == [[Image:Kamakura-gu Treasure.jpg|thumb|Prince Morinaga's statue at [[Kamakura-gū]] in Kamakura]] Prince Morinaga, with his prestige and his devotion to the civilian government cause, was Takauji's natural enemy and could count therefore on the support of his adversaries, among them Nitta Yoshisada, whom Takauji had offended. Tension between the Emperor and the Ashikaga gradually grew, until Takauji had Morinaga arrested on a pretext and first confined him in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], then transported him to Kamakura, where the Prince was kept prisoner until late August 1335. The situation in Kamakura continued to be tense, with Hōjō supporters staging sporadic revolts here and there. In the course of the same year [[Hōjō Tokiyuki]], son of last [[:en:Shikken|regent]] [[:en:Hōjō Takatoki|Takatoki]], tried to re-establish the shogunate by force and defeated Tadayoshi in Musashi, in today's [[:en:Kanagawa Prefecture|Kanagawa Prefecture]]. Tadayoshi had to flee, so before leaving he ordered the beheading of Prince Morinaga. Kamakura was therefore temporarily in Tokiyuki's hands. Heard the news, Takauji asked the Emperor to make him ''sei-i tai-shōgun'' so that he could quell the revolt and help his brother. When his request was denied, Takauji organized his forces and returned to Kamakura without the Emperor's permission, defeating the Hōjō.{{efn|Unlike every other source consulted Goble,{{sfn|Goble|1996}} on page 38 of his "History of Japan" (see references), [[:en:George Sansom|George Sansom]] states that Tokiyuki was killed on September 8, 1335 by Ashikaga forces entering Kamakura. This is also certainly an error.}} He then installed himself in Kamakura's [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]] neighborhood.Sansom says Ashikaga was staying at a temple called Eifuku-ji. This is an error, because Takauji in 1335 is known to have stayed at the ''[[:en:Bettō|Bettō]]'s'' residence at {{nihongo|[[Nikaidō#Etimology of the name|Yōfuku-ji]]|永福寺}}, a famous temple in Nikaidō built by Minamoto no Yoritomo which disappeared at some point during the 15th century. Yōfuku-ji was a traditional vacation residence of the ''shōguns'', and the characters in its name are indeed usually read "Eifuku-ji". See the article [[:en:Nikaidō|Nikaidō]]. When invited to return to Kyoto, he let it be known through his brother Tadayoshi that he felt safer where he was, and started to build himself a mansion in [[:en:Ōkura Bakufu|Ōkura]], where first Kamakura ''shōgun'' [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]]'s residence had been. == Civil war == Kyoto by then was aware that Takauji had assumed wide powers without imperial permission, for example nominating an [[Uesugi clan]] member to the post of Constable of Kōzuke, Nitta Yoshisada's native province. By late 1335 several thousand of the emperor's men were ready to go to Kamakura, while a great army at the command of [[:en:Kō no Moroyasu|Kō no Moroyasu]] was rushing there to help it resist the attack. On November 17, 1335, Tadayoshi issued a message in his brother's name asking all samurai to join the Ashikaga and destroy Nitta Yoshisada. The Court, meanwhile, had done the opposite, ordering samurai from all provinces to join Yoshisada and destroy the two Ashikaga. The war started with most samurai convinced that Takauji was the man they needed to have their grievances redressed, and most peasants were persuaded that they had been better off under the shogunate. The campaign was therefore enormously successful for the Ashikaga, with huge numbers of samurai rushing to join the two brothers. By February 23 of the following year Nitta Yoshisada and the Emperor had lost, and Kyoto itself had fallen. On February 25, 1336, Ashikaga Takauji entered the capital and the Kenmu Restoration ended. == Calendrical peculiarities of the era == The [[:en:Kenmu|Kenmu]] era is in the anomalous condition of having two different durations. Because [[:en:Japanese era name|Japanese era name]]s (''nengō'') change with the Emperor and the Imperial House split in two after 1336, the Kenmu era was counted by the two sides in two different ways. ''"Kenmu"'' is the era after the [[:en:Genkō (second)|Genkō]] era, and it is understood to have spanned the years 1334 through 1336 before the beginning of the ''"[[:en:Engen|Engen]]"'' era, as time was reckoned by the Southern Court; and it is concurrently said to have spanned the years 1334 through 1338 before [[:en:Ryakuō|Ryakuō]], as time was reckoned by the rival Northern Court. Because the Southern Court, the loser, is nonetheless considered the legitimate one, its time reckoning is the one used by historians. == See also == * [[List of the Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration|Fifteen Shrines of the Kenmu Restoration]] == Notes == {{notelist|1}} {{reflist|2}} == References == * {{cite book |last1=Hall| first1=John Whitney |last2=Duus |first2=Peter |title=The Cambridge History of Japan |editor=Yamamura Kozo |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |year=1990 |isbn=978-0-521-22354-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nT9CI5YQF_4C&q=kubo+kanto&pg=PA232}} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | year = 2008 | location = Kamakura, Japan | language = ja | isbn = 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} * {{cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan (3-volume boxed set) |publisher=Charles E. by [[:en:Ogata Gekkō|Ogata Gekkō]], 1890}} The {{nihongo|'''Kenmu Restoration'''|建武の新政|Kenmu no shinsei}} was a three-year period of [[:en:Imperial Court in Kyoto|Imperial]] rule in [[:en:Japanese history|Japanese history]] between the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] from 1333 to 1336.Spelling note: A modified [[:en:Hepburn romanization|Hepburn romanization]] system for Japanese words is used throughout Western publications in a range of languages including [[:en:English language|English]]. Unlike the standard system, it maintains the "''n''" even when it's followed by "[[:en:homorganic consonants|homorganic consonants]]" (e.g., ''shinbun'', not ''shimbun''). The Kenmu Restoration was an effort made by [[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]] to overthrow the ruling [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]] (''de facto'' ruled by [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō clan]]) and restore the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House]] to power in Japan, returning to [[:en:civilian government|civilian government]] after 148 years of ''[[:en:De facto|De facto]]'' [[:en:Military government|Military government]] from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]].Sansom 1977: 22-42. Go-Daigo launched the [[:en:Genkō War|Genkō War]] in 1331 against the Kamakura Shogunate but was defeated and forced to [[:en:Exile|Exile]] to the [[:en:Oki Islands|Oki Islands]]. Go-Daigo launched a second uprising, and with the assistance of the [[:en:defector|defected]] Kamakura general [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] and rebel leader [[Nitta Yoshisada]], defeated the Kamakura Shogunate at the [[:en:Siege of Kamakura (1333)|siege of Kamakura]] in 1333. The Imperial House was restored to power but Go-Daigo's policies failed to satisfy his major ''[[:en:Samurai|Samurai]]'' supporters and most Japanese people. The Kenmu Restoration was ultimately overthrown when Takauji became ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' and founded the [[:en:Ashikaga Shogunate|Ashikaga Shogunate]] in 1336, beginning the "[[:en:Nanboku-chō period|Northern and Southern Courts]]" period and the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]]. The Kenmu Restoration was the last time the [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]] held significant power until the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1868. == Background == The Emperor's role had been usurped by the [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] and [[:en:Hōjō clan|Hōjō]] families ever since [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] had obtained from the Emperor the title of ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' in 1192, ruling thereafter from [[:en:Kamakura|Kamakura]]. For various reasons, the Kamakura shogunate decided to allow two contending imperial lines—known as the [[Southern Court]] or junior line, and the [[:en:Northern Court|Northern Court]] or senior line—to alternate on the throne. The method worked for several successions until a member of the Southern Court ascended to the throne as Emperor Go-Daigo. Go-Daigo wanted to overthrow the shogunate and openly defied Kamakura by naming his own son his heir. In 1331 the shogunate exiled Go-Daigo but loyalist forces, including [[Kusunoki Masashige]], rebelled and came to his support. They were aided by, among others, future ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] who had turned against Kamakura when dispatched to put down Go-Daigo's rebellion. At roughly the same time, [[Nitta Yoshisada]], another eastern chieftain, attacked the shogunate's capital. The shogunate tried to resist his advance: Yoshisada and shogunate forces fought several times along the [[:en:Kamakura Kaidō|Kamakura Kaidō]], for example at {{nihongo|Kotesashigahara|小手差原}}, {{nihongo|Kumegawa|久米河}} (both near today's [[:en:Tokorozawa|Tokorozawa]], [[:en:Saitama Prefecture|Saitama Prefecture]]), and [[:en:Battle of Bubaigawara|Bubaigawara]], in today's [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū]], ever closer to Kamakura. The city was finally reached, [[:en:Siege of Kamakura (1333)|besieged]], and taken. Kamakura would remain for one century the political capital of the [[:en:Kantō region|Kantō region]], but its supremacy as political centre was over. == Objectives of the restoration == When Emperor Go-Daigo ascended the throne in 1318, he immediately manifested his intention to rule without interference from the military in Kamakura. Historical documents show that, disregarding evidence to the contrary, he and his advisers believed that a revival of the Imperial House was possible, and that the Kamakura's shogunate was the greatest and most obvious of the obstacles. Another situation that begged for a solution was the land-ownership problem posed by the manors and their lands (see the article [[shōen]]). The great landowners [[:en:Shugo|Shugo]] (governors) and [[:en:Jitō|Jitō]] (manor's lord), with their political independence and their tax exemptions were impoverishing the government and undermining its authority, and [[Kitabatake Chikafusa]], Go-Daigo's future chief adviser, discussed the situation in his works on succession. Chikafusa admitted that nobody had any intention of abolishing those privileges, so the hope of success on this front was from the beginning clearly very dim. What he planned to replace ''shugo'' and ''jitō'' with is unclear, but he surely had no intention of sharing power with the samurai class. However serious the land ownership problem, Go-Daigo and his advisers made no serious effort to solve it, partly because it was samurai from the manors in the western provinces that had defeated the shogunate for him. In such a situation, any effort to regulate the manors was bound to cause resentment among key allies. == Failure of Go-Daigo's policies == [[File:Emperor Godaigo by Monkan-bō Kōshin.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Emperor Go-Daigo|Emperor Go-Daigo]]]] The Emperor reclaimed the property of some manors his family had previously lost control of, rewarding them with, among others, Buddhist temples like [[Tō-ji]] and [[:en:Daitoku-ji|Daitoku-ji]] in the hope to obtain their support. He however failed to protect the rights of tenants and workers, whose complaints poured into the monasteries. He did not understand the importance to him of the warrior class either, because he never properly rewarded his minor samurai supporters, as he could have done using lands from the confiscated Hōjō lands, indulging instead in favoritism. These errors are the key to understanding the events of the next few decades. After rewarding religious institutions, he prepared to redistribute Hōjō lands, and samurai came to him in great numbers to lay their claims. The biggest rewards were given to samurai, among them [[Nitta Yoshisada]], the man who had destroyed the Kamakura shogunate, and [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]]. In so doing, however, he failed to return control of the provinces to [[Kuge|civilians]]. But he made his greatest error when he failed to properly reward minor warriors who had supported him. The tribunals set up to the purpose were inefficient and too inexperienced for the task, and corruption was rife. Samurai anger was made worse by the fact that Go-Daigo, wanting to build a palace for himself but having no funds, levied extra taxes from the samurai class. A wave of enmity towards the nobility started to run through the country, growing stronger with time. The [[Taiheiki]] also records that, although Takauji and Yoshisada were richly rewarded, the offices of ''shugo'' and ''jito'' in more than fifty [[:en:Provinces of Japan|provinces]] went to nobles and court bureaucrats, leaving no spoils for the warriors.Hall and Duus 1990: 184-7. By the end of 1335 the Emperor and the nobility had lost all support of the warrior class. == Rise of the Ashikaga brothers == [[Image:Ashikaga Takauji Jōdo-ji.jpg|thumb|A portrait of [[:en:Ashikaga Takauji|Ashikaga Takauji]] bearing his son [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshiakira|Yoshiakira]]'s cipher]] Go-Daigo wanted to re-establish his rule in Kamakura and the east of the country without sending a ''shōgun'' there, as this was seen as still too dangerous. As a compromise, he sent his six-year-old son Prince Norinaga to [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]] (the eastern part of today's [[:en:Tōhoku region|Tōhoku region]], stretching from [[:en:Fukushima Prefecture|Fukushima Prefecture]] in the south to [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori Prefecture]] in the north) and nominated him Governor-General of the Mutsu and [[:en:Dewa Province|Dewa Province]]s. In an obvious reply to this move, Ashikaga Takauji's younger brother [[:en:Ashikaga Tadayoshi|Tadayoshi]] without an order from the Emperor escorted another of his sons, eleven-year-old Nariyoshi (a.k.a. Narinaga) to Kamakura, where he installed him as Governor of the [[:en:Kōzuke Province|Kōzuke Province]] with himself as a deputy and de facto ruler.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo 2008: 24–25. The appointment of a warrior to an important post was intended to show the Emperor that the samurai class was not ready for a purely civilian rule. His only obstacle to the shogunate was Prince Morinaga. == Prince Morinaga == [[Image:Kamakura-gu Treasure.jpg|thumb|Prince Morinaga's statue at [[Kamakura-gū]] in Kamakura]] Prince Morinaga, with his prestige and his devotion to the civilian government cause, was Takauji's natural enemy and could count therefore on the support of his adversaries, among them Nitta Yoshisada, whom Takauji had offended. On February 25, 1336, Ashikaga Takauji entered the capital and the Kenmu Restoration ended. == Calendrical peculiarities of the era == The [[:en:Kenmu|Kenmu]] era is in the anomalous condition of having two different durations. Because [[:en:Japanese era name|Japanese era name]]s (''nengō'') change with the Emperor and the Imperial House split in two after 1336, the Kenmu era was counted by the two sides in two different ways. ''"Kenmu"'' is the era after the [[:en:Genkō (second)|Genkō]] era, and it is understood to have spanned the years 1334 through 1336 before the beginning of the ''"[[:en:Engen|Engen]]"'' era, as time was reckoned by the Southern Court; and it is concurrently said to have spanned the years 1334 through 1338 before [[:en:Ryakuō|Ryakuō]], as time was reckoned by the rival Northern Court.
